meta.title: Who really said "Success is to be measured not so much by the position one has reached as by the obstacles overcome"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Booker T. Washington wrote it, in The Outlook (1900) and Up from Slavery (1901). The popular form lightly trims his original sentence.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1856–1915 · Educator, orator & founder of Tuskegee Institute
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Washington’s. He wrote it in an article in The Outlook (10 November 1900) and reused it in his 1901 autobiography Up from Slavery ↗, Chapter II. The popular short form trims his original slightly — he wrote “the position that one has reached in life… the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “The Outlook,” 10 November 1900; then Up from Slavery, 1901 (ch. II)

source.excerpt: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ dates the line to Washington’s article in The Outlook, 10 November 1900, and confirms he deserves the credit.
The identical sentence appears in Up from Slavery ↗ (1901), Chapter II — verified verbatim against the Project Gutenberg text.
The circulating short form (“position one has reached… obstacles overcome”) is a genuine but lightly trimmed paraphrase of that sentence.
source.excerptNote: Washington’s original sentence, from Chapter II of Up from Slavery. The widely shared version condenses it to “the position one has reached… the obstacles overcome.”

author.name: Booker T. Washington
author.heading: About Booker T. Washington
author.metaLine: 1856–1915 · Educator, orator & founder of Tuskegee Institute
author.bio: Booker Taliaferro Washington was born into slavery in Virginia and rose to become the most influential Black American educator of his era, founding the Tuskegee Institute in 1881. His 1901 autobiography Up from Slavery became a landmark of American letters. This maxim distills the self-made ethic he preached and embodied.

misattribution.heading: A genuine quote, lightly reworded
misattribution.intro: The attribution is correct — the wording is what shifts. The version that circulates on quote sites is a condensed form of Washington’s original sentence.

items.why: Sites drop “that one has reached in life” and the closing clause “which he has overcome while trying to succeed,” leaving “the position one has reached… the obstacles overcome.” The meaning is faithful; only the phrasing is trimmed, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Booker T. Washington genuinely wrote this in Up from Slavery ↗ (1901), first in The Outlook (1900) — the popular version just tightens his original words.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Washington wrote the line in The Outlook in 1900 and folded it into Up from Slavery, where it caps a reflection on his boyhood. Born into slavery, he framed achievement not as a rank attained but as a measure of the distance travelled against resistance.
The maxim became one of his most-quoted lines precisely because his own life embodied it — from salt furnace and coal mine to founder of Tuskegee and adviser to presidents.
context.pull: Not the position reached, but the obstacles overcome.
